article.title: What if the polls are wrong again?
article.subtitle: Systematic polling errors are common. Polls might be biased against Republicans again. Or against Democrats.

extraction.summary: Model Talk on systematic polling error and the difference between hedging and 'unskewing'. Since 2008, polls had a systematic anti-Democratic bias once (2012), anti-Republican four times (2014, 2016, 2020, 2024) and were unbiased four times, which is hard to distinguish from chance. The Trump-era anti-Republican bias, averaging 3.8 points, appears only on presidential dates; midterms were unbiased and off-year and special elections were 1.3 points biased toward Republicans. The article describes FLIPR's four uncertainty layers, its house-effect and fundamentals adjustments, and its core 'party-neutral' constraint: forecast errors can be correlated but their direction is unpredictable. It also offers a turnout-and-nonresponse theory for why polling bias differs between high- and low-turnout elections.

findings.statement: FLIPR's core constraint is that the forecast is 'party-neutral'. Polling averages may be predictably biased, for example a red state's polls understating the Republican or a blue state's understating the Democrat, and fundamentals correct for that. But the direction of error in the blended forecast is assumed unpredictable; no party-specific assumption such as 'polls always underestimate Republicans' is built in, which Silver would call unskewing.
findings.rationale: Past directional biases are consistent with chance given small effective samples.
findings.evidence_quote: we assume that the direction of the bias of our polling averages might be predictable, but the direction of the bias in our blended forecasts (polls + fundamentals + expert ratings) isn’t predictable.

findings.statement: FLIPR simulates four layers of polling uncertainty: (1) a uniform national error across all races; (2) demographically or geographically correlated errors, e.g. Democrats beat polls among Hispanics but Republicans in the Midwest; (3) a statewide error shared by a state's Senate, governor and House races; (4) a single-race error. In presidential years most uncertainty sits in layer 1, while in midterms it is more evenly spread across the four.
findings.rationale: Midterm errors in 2018 and 2022 were largely unbiased overall but regionally significant.
findings.evidence_quote: For the midterms, they’re more evenly distributed between the four layers.

findings.statement: In Silver Bulletin's pollster database, a simple average of all polls in the final three weeks of the 2016, 2020 and 2024 general elections overestimated Democrats by 3.8 points. Midterm polls in 2018 and 2022 were almost completely unbiased in aggregate, and off-year and special election polls in the Trump years were biased toward Republicans by 1.3 points on average.
findings.evidence_quote: they overestimated Democrats by a margin of 3.8 percentage points.

findings.statement: In the nine cycles since 2008, polls were systematically biased against Democrats once (2012, by about 3 points with Obama beating RCP averages in all 11 toss-up states), against Republicans four times (2014, 2016, 2020, 2024), and roughly unbiased four times. Five biased cycles splitting 4-1 happens 37.5 percent of the time with a fair coin.
findings.evidence_quote: if you flip a fair coin 5 times, then 37.5 percent of the time, either heads or tails will come up at least 4 out of 5 times.

findings.statement: FLIPR does not assume any individual poll is unbiased: its house-effects adjustment pulls firms with systematic D-vs-R differences, such as Marist's Democratic-leaning 2026 numbers, toward the consensus.
findings.evidence_quote: FLIPR adjusts their polls to be closer to the consensus, as we do with any firm that shows these systematic differences.

findings.statement: Race-level polls are blended with fundamentals that reflect state partisanship: in South Carolina, a polling average of Graham +2.6 became a forecast of Graham +5.3. By symmetry, Democrats are expected to outperform their polls in blue states such as Minnesota.
findings.evidence_quote: our forecast shows Graham winning by 5.3 after blending in fundamentals that account for how red South Carolina usually is.

findings.statement: Treating state polling errors as independent coin flips is the key modeling mistake: because FiveThirtyEight modeled correlation, it gave Trump 29 percent in 2016 while coin-flip models gave him 1 percent or less. Correlation matters most among demographically similar states; in 2016, a miss with non-college whites concentrated in Midwestern swing states decided the race while national polls were fairly accurate.
findings.evidence_quote: Precisely because it didn’t do this, FiveThirtyEight’s final forecast gave Trump a 29 percent chance in 2016

findings.statement: In the final 2024 Silver Bulletin presidential forecast (about 50/50), the single most likely scenario was Trump sweeping all seven swing states, which happened, and the second most likely was Harris sweeping all seven, reflecting correlated errors.
findings.evidence_quote: But the single most likely scenario was Trump sweeping all seven key swing states

findings.statement: Error correlation lies on a spectrum: presidential years are near uniform national swing; congressional races in presidential years are in between, with coattails and party-line voting; midterms are in the middle; off-year, runoff and special elections are near independent coin flips and produce many surprises, such as Scott Brown in 2010 and Doug Jones in 2017. Many 2026 FLIPR changes sharpened the presidential-year versus midterm distinction.
findings.evidence_quote: Presidential years are very much on the “uniform swing” side of that spectrum whereas midterms are somewhere in the middle.

findings.statement: Since 2016 the Silver Bulletin database includes 246 qualifying polls covering 36 special/off-year races across 27 election dates; Democrats usually did better than these polls predicted. Larger historical midterm polling errors exist in the deeper archive, e.g. 1994 and 1998.
findings.evidence_quote: since 2016, a total of 246 qualifying polls covering 36 distinct races across 27 unique election dates.

findings.statement: Silver's theory, not built into FLIPR, which makes no turnout assumptions about bias direction: polls oversample enthusiastic and high-social-trust respondents who are also more likely to vote. In high-turnout presidential elections the oversampling dominates and low-propensity Trump voters are missed; in low-turnout elections those voters also stay home, and pollster corrections may overcorrect.
findings.evidence_quote: FLIPR doesn’t actually make any assumptions about turnout.

findings.statement: A truly random sample is impossible today: people screen calls and online panels cannot be randomly pinged. Pollsters weight demographically (e.g. education, race) to correct nonresponse, but partisan and enthusiasm-driven nonresponse is a mixed bag because self-selection also acts as a de facto likely-voter screen. Silver calls the 2024 Selzer Iowa poll the last gasp of traditional telephone polls that made little effort to correct for partisan nonresponse.
findings.evidence_quote: The dirty little secret of polling these days is that it’s impossible to get a truly random sample of voters.

findings.statement: In early FiveThirtyEight years the polling averages were an intermediate step in the model and not always surfaced publicly; Silver Bulletin now displays polling averages separately and then blends them with other information.
findings.evidence_quote: In the earlier FiveThirtyEight years, our models basically did the same thing, but the polling averages were more of an intermediate accounting step

findings.statement: FiveThirtyEight's 2012 model called every state correctly, but its internal diagnostics gave only a slim chance of a perfect score (Florida was about 50/50). Correct calls can mask margin errors; 2012 polls overestimated Romney by about 3 points.
findings.evidence_quote: Our internal diagnostics gave us only a slim chance of getting a perfect score.

political_insights.insight: In the Trump era college-educated voters are more likely to answer polls and to vote Democratic, while non-college whites lean heavily Republican; failing to weight by education caused the 2016 Midwest miss.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Weight or model by education; expect correlated errors among non-college-heavy states.

political_insights.insight: Democrats have generally outperformed polls and expectations in Trump-era special and off-year elections.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Special elections are leading indicators but with independent, noisy errors.

open_questions: Relative variance assigned to each of the four error layers in midterms vs presidential years.
